knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE,
                      fig.align = "center", out.width = "90%")

needed <- c("ggplot2", "rpart", "rpart.plot", "randomForest", "pROC", "knitr")

# Question and intended use

**Question:** Which employees are likely to leave, and which measured patterns are useful for identifying them before departure?

A human-resources team could use the answer to prioritize retention conversations and targeted workplace improvements. This is a decision-support model, not an automatic employment decision.

# Data and cleaning

```{r read-data}
url <- paste0("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/IBM/",
              "employee-attrition-aif360/master/data/emp_attrition.csv")

d <- read.csv(url, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
names(d)[1] <- "Age"

cat("Original dimensions:", nrow(d), "rows and", ncol(d), "columns\n")

constant_cols <- names(d)[vapply(d, function(x) {
  length(unique(x[!is.na(x)])) <= 1
}, logical(1))]
constant_cols

identifier_cols <- "EmployeeNumber"
d <- d[, !(names(d) %in% c(constant_cols, identifier_cols)), drop = FALSE]

cat("Duplicate rows:", sum(duplicated(d)), "\n")
cat("Missing values:", sum(is.na(d)), "\n")

d$Attrition <- factor(d$Attrition, levels = c("No", "Yes"))
character_cols <- vapply(d, is.character, logical(1))
d[character_cols] <- lapply(d[character_cols], factor)

cat("Clean dimensions:", nrow(d), "rows and", ncol(d), "columns\n")
```

The file arrived with 1,470 records and 35 variables. I repaired the stray character in the first column name. `EmployeeCount`, `Over18`, and `StandardHours` contain one value for every record, while `EmployeeNumber` is only an identifier; all four are removed. There are no missing values. Duplicate rows are checked after the identifier and constants are removed. The positive class is `Attrition = Yes`.

```{r response-summary}
tab <- table(d$Attrition)
tab
prop.table(tab)
```

# Exploratory plots

```{r overtime-plot, fig.cap="Attrition is more common for employees who work overtime."}
ggplot(d, aes(x = OverTime, fill = Attrition)) +
  geom_bar(position = "fill") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent_format()) +
  labs(title = "Attrition by Overtime",
       x = "Works overtime", y = "Within-group proportion") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("No" = "#56B4E9", "Yes" = "#E69F00"))
```

Overtime status is strongly associated with attrition: a larger proportion of overtime employees left. This motivates including job demands and workload in the model.

```{r tenure-plot, fig.cap="Attrition varies with tenure and is most visible among employees with fewer years at the company."}
ggplot(d, aes(x = YearsAtCompany, fill = Attrition)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 2, position = "fill", boundary = 0) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent_format()) +
  labs(title = "Attrition by Years at Company",
       x = "Years at the company", y = "Within-bin proportion") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("No" = "#56B4E9", "Yes" = "#E69F00"))
```

The proportion leaving appears to be highest in some early-tenure ranges. This is a useful pattern, although tenure should not be interpreted as a cause.

# Training and test split

```{r split}
yes_idx <- which(d$Attrition == "Yes")
no_idx  <- which(d$Attrition == "No")

test_yes <- sample(yes_idx, floor(0.30 * length(yes_idx)))
test_no  <- sample(no_idx,  floor(0.30 * length(no_idx)))
test_idx <- c(test_yes, test_no)

train <- d[-test_idx, ]
test  <- d[test_idx, ]

cat("Training:", nrow(train), "; test:", nrow(test), "\n")
cat("Training attrition:\n")
print(prop.table(table(train$Attrition)))
cat("Test attrition:\n")
print(prop.table(table(test$Attrition)))
```

The split occurs before fitting any model. Because the response is uneven, I stratify by `Attrition` so both the training and test sets retain approximately the original class proportions.

# Classification models

## Full decision tree

```{r full-tree}
full_tree <- rpart(Attrition ~ ., data = train, method = "class",
                   control = rpart.control(cp = 0, minsplit = 20,
                                           minbucket = 10, xval = 10))

cat("Full tree leaves:", length(unique(full_tree$where)), "\n")
full_prob <- predict(full_tree, test, type = "prob")[, "Yes"]
full_pred <- factor(ifelse(full_prob >= 0.50, "Yes", "No"),
                    levels = c("No", "Yes"))
```

## Pruned decision tree

```{r prune-tree}
cp_table <- full_tree$cptable
min_xerr_row <- which.min(cp_table[, "xerror"])
min_xerr <- cp_table[min_xerr_row, "xerror"]
se <- cp_table[min_xerr_row, "xstd"]
eligible <- cp_table[, "xerror"] <= min_xerr + se
prune_row <- which(eligible)[1]
chosen_cp <- cp_table[prune_row, "CP"]
chosen_cp

pruned_tree <- prune(full_tree, cp = chosen_cp)
pruned_prob <- predict(pruned_tree, test, type = "prob")[, "Yes"]
pruned_pred <- factor(ifelse(pruned_prob >= 0.50, "Yes", "No"),
                      levels = c("No", "Yes"))

cat("Pruned tree leaves:", length(unique(pruned_tree$where)), "\n")
rpart.plot(pruned_tree, extra = 104, box.palette = "-RdBu",
           main = "Pruned decision tree")
```

The tree is pruned with the 1-standard-error rule. This favors a simpler tree whose cross-validation error is within one standard error of the minimum.

## Bagging

```{r bagging}
bag_predictions <- matrix(0, nrow = nrow(test), ncol = 100)

for (b in 1:100) {
  boot_idx <- sample(seq_len(nrow(train)), nrow(train), replace = TRUE)
  boot_train <- train[boot_idx, ]
  bag_fit <- rpart(Attrition ~ ., data = boot_train, method = "class",
                   control = rpart.control(cp = 0.01, minsplit = 20,
                                           minbucket = 10))
  bag_predictions[, b] <- predict(bag_fit, test, type = "prob")[, "Yes"]
}

bag_prob <- rowMeans(bag_predictions)
bag_pred <- factor(ifelse(bag_prob >= 0.50, "Yes", "No"),
                   levels = c("No", "Yes"))
```

## Random forest

```{r random-forest}
rf_fit <- randomForest(Attrition ~ ., data = train,
                       ntree = 500, mtry = floor(sqrt(ncol(train) - 1)),
                       importance = TRUE)
rf_prob <- predict(rf_fit, test, type = "prob")[, "Yes"]
rf_pred <- predict(rf_fit, test, type = "response")
```

# Performance comparison

```{r roc-and-table}
metric_row <- function(name, truth, prob, pred) {
  cm <- table(Predicted = pred, Actual = truth)
  tp <- cm["Yes", "Yes"]
  tn <- cm["No", "No"]
  fp <- cm["Yes", "No"]
  fn <- cm["No", "Yes"]
  roc_obj <- pROC::roc(truth, prob, levels = c("No", "Yes"),
                       direction = "<", quiet = TRUE)
  data.frame(
    Model = name,
    Accuracy = (tp + tn) / sum(cm),
    Sensitivity = tp / (tp + fn),
    Specificity = tn / (tn + fp),
    PPV = tp / (tp + fp),
    NPV = tn / (tn + fn),
    AUC = as.numeric(pROC::auc(roc_obj)),
    row.names = NULL
  )
}

comparison <- rbind(
  metric_row("Full tree", test$Attrition, full_prob, full_pred),
  metric_row("Pruned tree", test$Attrition, pruned_prob, pruned_pred),
  metric_row("Bagging", test$Attrition, bag_prob, bag_pred),
  metric_row("Random forest", test$Attrition, rf_prob, rf_pred)
)

majority_outcome <- names(sort(table(test$Attrition), decreasing = TRUE))[1]
majority_accuracy <- max(prop.table(table(test$Attrition)))
comparison <- rbind(
  data.frame(Model = "Majority class benchmark",
             Accuracy = majority_accuracy,
             Sensitivity = if (majority_outcome == "Yes") 1 else 0,
             Specificity = if (majority_outcome == "No") 1 else 0,
             PPV = if (majority_outcome == "Yes") majority_accuracy else 0,
             NPV = if (majority_outcome == "No") majority_accuracy else 0,
             AUC = 0.50),
  comparison
)

comparison[, -1] <- lapply(comparison[, -1], function(x) round(x, 3))
kable(comparison, caption = "Test-set comparison (0.50 probability threshold)")
```

The benchmark always predicts `No`, the more common class. It is useful because ordinary accuracy can look acceptable while failing to identify leavers. In this setting, a false negative means that a likely leaver receives no retention intervention, while a false positive means resources may be spent on an employee who would have stayed. The threshold should be reviewed against the cost of those two errors; a threshold lower than 0.50 may be appropriate if missed leavers are expensive.

```{r roc-plot, fig.cap="ROC curves for the four fitted models on the test set."}
plot(pROC::roc(test$Attrition, full_prob, levels = c("No", "Yes"),
               direction = "<", quiet = TRUE),
     col = "#999999", lwd = 2, main = "ROC curves")
plot(pROC::roc(test$Attrition, pruned_prob, levels = c("No", "Yes"),
               direction = "<", quiet = TRUE),
     col = "#0072B2", lwd = 2, add = TRUE)
plot(pROC::roc(test$Attrition, bag_prob, levels = c("No", "Yes"),
               direction = "<", quiet = TRUE),
     col = "#D55E00", lwd = 2, add = TRUE)
plot(pROC::roc(test$Attrition, rf_prob, levels = c("No", "Yes"),
               direction = "<", quiet = TRUE),
     col = "#009E73", lwd = 2, add = TRUE)
legend("bottomright", legend = c("Full tree", "Pruned tree", "Bagging", "Random forest"),
       col = c("#999999", "#0072B2", "#D55E00", "#009E73"),
       lwd = 2, bty = "n")
```

AUC measures the probability that a randomly selected leaver receives a higher score than a randomly selected employee who stays. A value of 0.50 means no ranking ability, while 1.00 means perfect ranking.

# Recommendation and limitations

Choose the model only after checking whether sensitivity or false-negative cost is the main criterion. The random forest and bagging may have similar discrimination, so a few percentage points of test accuracy should not by themselves be treated as a meaningful winner. A one-time test split is not enough to establish deployment reliability; cross-validation or repeated splits would add uncertainty estimates.

Use the model to guide supportive human review, not automatic firing or denial of opportunities. Attrition is observational, so predictive relationships do not establish causation. Protected or sensitive attributes—especially `Age`, `Gender`, and `MaritalStatus`—require fairness review before operational use. A next step would be calibration and a cost-based threshold selected with HR.
